utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Mr. Oric, can you following the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and also good morning to my learned friends of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. In my team also, Mrs. Patricia Sellers, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our acting case manager, Ms. Sanja Bokulic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to the learned friends from the OTP. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries before we bring in the witness? Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, we have some documents to tender. I give the floor to Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution would like to submit, to tender some replacement exhibits that were submitted to the Court on November 29th when Mr. Mirsad Mustafic testified, so I would like to hand those up, again as replacement documents. We have complete sets beginning with Prosecution Exhibit P600. I believe with respect to this document the last page was missing. And the next, Prosecution Exhibit P605 --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And with respect to P605, Your Honour, I'd just like to state for the record that we are submitting the additional pages to this exhibit and that is ERN 03425954 and 03426125. The previous pages were submitted, and that -- those are 03925949 and 5951. And that's a complete set of that particular exhibit. And also we have Prosecution Exhibit P607, and this is a complete translation of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're not particularly happy or clear about what this procedure is, about exhibits replacing other exhibits. The witness might have had something to say about additional pages. It's something certainly we're reserving our position. It's entirely new to us. And so before any replacement takes place, we'd appreciate it if you would hear our submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have a problem with that. With respect to the final exhibit that we just submitted, it's a --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: A complete -- right, correct. That's a complete translation and simply a replacement of the previous exhibit. We've had a chance to revise the translation that we submitted before. I don't think the Defence would have a problem with that. But of course they can put the objection on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the position will be as follows. We expect to hear back from you, Mr. Jones, if you have an objection. When I say "Mr. Jones," or Madam Vidovic, if you have an objection about having these three documents replacing the previous ones. For the time being, of course the previous ones will remain in the record, and the matter will become final when we meet again in January. If we have not heard any objection on your part. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And finally, Your Honour, we do have CDs for the Trial Chamber. These are copies of the Oric interview, Prosecution Exhibit 328 and P329. The Defence already received their copies. So we'd like to tender these to the Court. It's a part of P328 and P329. We understand that there was a problem with the previous CDs, so we're replacing those. And as I say, before the Defence already received their copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you can hand them over to our respective secretaries later on. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Ms. Richardson has completed what she wanted to say, we have an -- a matter that is of earlier date which we would like to raise today. Yesterday at about 9.30 in the evening, 12 CDs were placed in our locker, and could the receipt number 266A be distributed to everyone so that Their Honours can follow our discussion. These CDs -- or rather, one of these CDs containing -- contains documents, and 11 CDs contain video footages. All of them were delivered to Defence under Rule 66(B) and 68 and relate to witness Tony Odly [as interpreted]. As you know, the witness should start testifying the day after tomorrow. Your Honours, I stated Tony Birtley. It hasn't been entered clearly into the transcript. He should begin his testimony the day after tomorrow, which means -- or rather, tomorrow, my colleague has drawn my attention to that fact. We literally have only this afternoon to review the CDs and to proof the witness. What transpires from the annex is that the Defence -- the material was provided to the Defence as a result of the ISU searches. Your Honours, I have no more words to express our dissatisfaction with the way the OTP proceeds in relation to their obligations under Rule 68. As I stated, these materials were delivered to us both under Rule 66(B) and under Rule 68; therefore, exculpatory material. I reviewed this morning only one of these CDs and was quite shocked by the contents. I could see there are many persons who were repeatedly mentioned in the course of this trial, including some of our witnesses. Your Honours, had we had the material before, we would certainly have used in the best interests of our client. We have simply been deprived of the possibility to use the material. If you recall - and this matter was raised on several occasions - our first request to the Prosecutor was to be supplied with all the video materials which had to do with the situation in Srebrenica. From the very start, we also asked to be given material concerning our witnesses. Mr. Birtley figured on our list already in June this year, and I can't see why these searches had not been carried out earlier. I believe this brings us again into a very difficult situation which poses great concern to us because we cannot properly prepare Mr. Tony Birtley's -- prepare for Mr. Tony Birtley's testimony. Your Honours, I don't know what else I should do to remedy this situation that has arisen as a result of the OTP's actions concerning Rule 68. We have done our best. We have used all our resources to utilise the materials we received in respect of our witnesses as best we could. I hope that I have been quite clear, and I will give the floor to my colleague now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted to add one matter, Your Honour. I'm actually dealing with these next two witnesses, Colonel Dudley and Tony Birtley. We have an extremely short space of time to proof these witnesses. It really is a matter of one afternoon with Tony Birtley. We've spent, in preparing for this trial, countless hours reviewing video material that we already have to see if there's anything in which a witness appears, so we can put it to him, so we can get his reaction. In just the five minutes when I was looking over the shoulder of our CaseMap manager, who was just quickly reviewing the files, I see even this witness who is coming today talking to the camera -- it's something I have never seen before. It's -- basically there's a whole video, I can tell you just looking at it, of what is known as rushes, unedited material, taken by Tony Birtley, a witness who is coming either tomorrow or the day after tomorrow. I have got no opportunity now to actually show this material to Lieutenant Colonel Dudley. I have also seen at least three or four Defence witnesses, and in that I include people who were on the Defence list at one point and who if we had seen video material in which they are speaking it might have made difference, a Rule 92 bis witness I've seen. And this is in the last five minutes just looking over the shoulder of my colleague. That's one CD. There are 12 CDs. Why on earth didn't the Prosecution do this at the start of the trial? Why on earth didn't they do it when they received our witness list? The very day that a witness is starting saying, here you go, Defence, here are 12 CDs. It will take two or three days for us to look through it, to get through that material. And it's just impossible. I don't see how we are going to do our job under these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's hear what the Prosecution has to say on this. And then Madam Vidovic or Mr. Jones, or both of you, please tell us what you want. Yes, who is going to deal with this? Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Let me first put forward that when we had to deal with a certain witness and try to elicit the relevant material from a Defence witness to review it with a view to our obligations, 66(B) and 68, meaning 66(B) to enable the Defence to inspect our books, and 68 to convey that to the Defence. Firstly, the material handed over indeed include Rule 68, but only recently it came to my knowledge that such material was included in the videos handed over, meaning also that I can understand that it is a hardship to examine this material by the Defence because I know it for myself how it is and how voluminous the material is. At the same time, it might enable me to sit down with the Defence after this proceeding today and to point out the particular parts of the video that underline to me that there is potential Rule 68 material in it. When it comes to the submission that why not in an earlier stage? Well, we learned only in the later stage of trial of course that Birtley was a -- should be on the Defence witness list, but he's not the only one. There were a lot of witnesses and all this triggered the material. And you can't process it at once; you have to do it in a kind of schedule. And unfortunately this witness triggered a lot of material, material which the Defence should also be aware of when they are dealing with the witness because why was the material triggered from -- by the ISU because of the very fact that he is a journalist who made a lot of -- who shot a lot of video footages and is referred to by his name in it and thus triggered by the ISU. Meaning, it's not that I put the accent that the Defence could know already by themselves all the footages that their witness shot, but it's also a matter of knowing and being triggered by the very fact and being aware that the Defence put a witness on the list that has to do with a lot of material from a professional point of view that he shot, including his contribution to the documentary and his well-known documentary "Cry from the Grave." This is what I can offer: To sit down with the Defence and to point out what I know about the parts that include Rule 68, and thus enabling them to immediately go to that aspect of the material provided, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, you're suggesting that as far as identification of Rule 68 material, rather than they go through the tapes themselves and decide for themselves what is exculpatory or not --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- they rely on you, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, not to rely on me. That's their own discretion to find for themselves. But I indicated in reviewing the material the parts that underlines Rule 68. And that might help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do it this way. We are going to do the following. We are going to give you ten minutes within which, if you want, you sit down and talk if there is a possibility of a solution. But I see Mr. Jones already saying, no, there is no possibility of any such thing. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, no, it's -- Your Honour, it's simply with the greatest respect, that I don't think ten minutes now would lead to a solution. May I just say the following that, one, Mr. Wubben has just said about the fact that there are a lot of material and the Prosecution has just discovered it. We will excuse any situation that we're in no matter how unfair to the Defence because that's always -- we could have 200 CDs deposited on our door and be told that, well, there's a lot of material and it's just been discovered. There has to be some remedy in it for the accused to have a fair trial. There has to be something which is done -- may I just -- Your Honour, I just have two further points. If there's material in these videos which could have impeached Prosecution witnesses, or which could have supported our witnesses, there has to be a remedy for that. It can't be that that situation is just allowed to occur, and there's nothing for the Defence, no remedy whatsoever. As far as the two matters mentioned by Mr. Wubben, the part of a well-known documentary. I don't know how well-known the documentary is, but what I was seeing was unedited rushes and that's simply -- that's stuff which hasn't been broadcast at all. I don't want it to be thought that this is in the public domain. As far as sitting down is concerned, with the Prosecution, we have to proof this witness this afternoon. We have a very short space of time, we need to get on with that, and we have found throughout this trial that we have a different view of what's Rule 68 exculpatory from the Prosecution, and that's why I submit it wouldn't be worth our while to sit down with the Prosecution and have the Prosecution point out what they consider is exculpatory. We're in a better position to do that, but we need to do it. And so, one, I mean, it's for Your Honours to ensure that the Trial Chamber makes sure the Prosecution complies with its obligations. I can't think of a remedy now, apart from the fact that the Prosecution shouldn't use any of this material either with this witness or with Tony Birtley, because we really -- we do have a right to review all of this material, and it is 12 CDs and will take two or three days to look at, and that surely would be the most unfair, if on top of everything else this is used in a cross-examination before we've even had a chance to analyse it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is your specific -- or what are your specific requests, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Simply for the Trial Chamber to take whatever action you deem appropriate to make sure that the Prosecution complies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is Mr. Birtley already here?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll withdraw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Could I ask Mr. Wubben, how long time to you foresee such conversation or meeting with the Defence would take for you to point out what the Prosecution think is its obligation in relation to 68?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I think -- Your Honour, I think that it should be done within an hour. It means that I point on very documents this is what I -- what my opinion is as a part of Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: May I also have a question to both parties. If I understood you correctly, Mr. Wubben, you suggested that you would indicate to the Defence those parts of the videos which you think are exculpatory. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Exculpatory, in my opinion, and just to support the quick pointing out of any potential relevant part of it rather than to go immediately through all of them. And, by the way, we don't have transcripts for the rushes, but I can, for myself, note down which part of it -- of that footage might be relevant in that respect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Then I have a question to the Defence. Is it your position that this would not help you sufficiently because you cannot completely rely on what has been indicated to you by the Prosecution? You want to go through all videos in order to find out whether there is any exculpatory material?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's a combination of the two. It's due to the amount of time that actually sitting down and doing this would not be useful -- a good use of our time. If in writing, and I would suggest the Prosecution could put in writing, which parts are exculpatory and then we can simply take that and then look for those parts. But we will, obviously, have to look through the whole -- all of the CDs because it's a question -- not just of exculpatory but of how else this material might be used by the Prosecution with our coming witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The problem is that -- I don't look at these CDs only from the Rule 68 perspective. I have to look at them wholistically, once they are disclosed or they are in the possession of the Defence. The Defence have to have the opportunity to go through them in their entirety because a question that could be asked need not necessarily be related to Rule 68 material. But I think in my mind, it is very obviously. However, something which is out of courtesy, much more important than this at the moment. Usher, could you please escort into the courtroom Lieutenant Colonel Dudley and the representatives of the US embassy, because I need to explain to them that they need to wait a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Dudley, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. Mr. Johnson and Madam Schildge, good morning to you too. I've got some good news and some bad news. The good news is at some later point in time we will hear the testimony of Lieutenant Dudley. The bad news has already been communicated when I said "at some later point in time." We have a problem. The problem does not relate -- please make yourself comfortable, Lieutenant. The problem does not relate to the lieutenant or to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel. The problem is in relation to some fresh documents that have come to the surface this morning which the Defence have not had time to go through and we need to clear this up before we can even start with the testimony of Lieutenant Colonel Dudley. So my apologies to you and to you, sir. I hope you understand. It's not something that we were anticipating; we were not anticipating it in the least, and we actually were praying that nothing of the sort will happen again, but it has happened and we need to address it and decide it in the first place. Also because some of these documents could possibly be used during the examination-in-chief or cross-examination of this witness. So we will be withdrawing to my Chamber shortly, and we need some time to think and deliberate on this matter and then come back with a decision. Of course we will then proceed with the testimony of Lieutenant Colonel Dudley. But we cannot start with that before we decide on this issue which also impacts on whether we should be -- we would be hearing the next witness then. All right? So I ask you to be kind enough to bear with us and please accept our apologies. This is something that was thrown upon us this morning quite unexpectedly and which we have to deal with. Lieutenant Colonel, my apologies to you. Thank you. We will now withdraw and we'll come back and we'll communicate to you as soon as -- with you as soon as we are ready to start. --- Break taken at 9.50 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we tell you how we propose to handle this matter, are there any further statements that you would like to make? Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, I want to make it clear to this Trial Chamber. I stated that we don't have transcripts for the rushes. That means that when it comes to a review by the Prosecution for Rule 68 material, that we were able to -- in this schedule of time -- we were able to disclose the rushes but not able to define within these B/C/S -- within the B/C/S language the parts of Rule 68. So we did make -- we were able to review the documents, the hard copy of the documents, but not the rushes by itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it's just to say in the meantime we've carried on reviewing two of the CDs, and we've now see Becir Bogilovic, Tony Birtley, Colonel Dudley, Thierry Pontus, Donald Paris, Captain McDonald, Ilijav Pilav. We've seen all those people just in the last time. Just so Your Honour appreciates what we're dealing with in terms of this video, including an interview with Lieutenant Colonel Dudley which I have never seen before until now and which is exculpatory and which I might have used with him. In terms of solution, perhaps the only solution at this point is that we want to continue with Tony Birtley. It's very difficult -- it's been very difficult getting him here. It would be impossible to get him back, and that the Prosecution not be allowed to use any of this material with this witness today or Tony Birtley, then at least we're not taken off guard because we do need two or three days to review this material. That's all I'd submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a position on what has just been stated by Mr. Jones, Mr. Wubben? Are you prepared to not use any of the material in your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: When the Defence is not able to use the material with Tony Birtley, so it's only a fair with a view to equality of arms not to be used by the Prosecution as well, including, of course, today Mr. Dudley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But does that cure or remedy the position from the Defence point of view? Because the Defence can always come back and say it did not have the opportunity to examine Mr. Birtley, as we would have had we been privy to the contents of those tapes beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence should be in the position to fully proof Mr. Birtley. If they have not that position with a view to the volume of the material, it should be given their position, regardless of the planning for scheduling by the end of the week, then it must be in part proofing and enabling the Defence to -- in a later stage to call him on the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So our position is as follows -- there are various options, actually, mainly two. Option number one is the following. Particularly hearing what Mr. Jones has just stated that at least in one or two of the tapes that they managed to glance through quickly, there is, for example, an interview with the witness we are about to start hearing, Lieutenant Colonel Dudley. Position -- option one would be the following. That we will not start with Colonel -- Lieutenant Colonel Dudley today, but we'll start with him tomorrow, during which time the Defence would have an opportunity, at least to see whether there is any material that they would like to put to Lieutenant Dudley, with the proviso, assuming that they would not be in a position to go through all this material, their position will be reserved to bring back Colonel Dudley at a later stage if they need to put more questions to him. Accompanied with this would be that it's fully understandable that it's -- the Defence requires time to go through all this and proof Tony Birtley, that we don't hear the testimony of Tony Birtley at all, and we'll make sure that he comes back at some later point in time to give evidence when the Defence are in a position to go through his testimony after proper proofing, taking into consideration also the -- so that's option one, note only Birtley evidence testimony this week. Delay of Colonel Dudley's testimony until the Defence is in a position to go ahead with a proper examination. That's option number one. Option number two is the following. We go ahead with the two witnesses as scheduled with the following -- under the following conditions. Condition number one is that the Defence will not at any time use these tapes or documents or whatever they are, exhibits, in their cross-examination while either of these two witnesses are testifying now and -- that the Prosecution, yeah, will -- I'm sorry. I apologise to you. Prosecution will not make use of these documents, as requested, et cetera. And the Defence will have the absolute right to have these two witnesses re-called at a later stage to continue testifying on any matter that the Defence may choose to examine them upon. These are the two options, the two practical options, that we foresee. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then obviously if there is a re-call, this embargo on the Prosecution to make use will be lifted. Obviously then it will be possible for the Prosecution to make use of. These are the two options that -- we see there are other options, obviously, but we tried to approach this matter in as positive a manner as possible, trying to find a -- the most practical solution. One is maybe practical -- more practical than the other from one respect, and the same could be said to the other solution, may be practical than the other from a approach. I think before we decide what to do, we would like to know if you have a preference to either of these two. And I would imagine you have a preference for the second?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we certainly favour option two. And I should emphasise that we really -- there is the risk that we would lose Tony Birtley altogether if we don't bring him now. He is moving to the other side of the world. And he -- I know his commitments in the coming months and so -- so that's one matter and the fact that they're here, that we want to make progress, we would certainly prefer option two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But with this reservation -- and I'll make it clear to Mr. Birtley that he will need to come over if there is need for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I take it that we don't use the -- any of such documents disclosed whenever Defence cannot locate those documents or choose to use those documents for examination-in-chief of Tony Birtley, that we also should not use those documents or videos. But whenever a particular video or document has been chosen, that we are entitled to use that particular document as well during or cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I think -- I think this is simple enough not to require any explanation. If in the process of the examination-in-chief of either Colonel -- Lieutenant Colonel Dudley or Mr. Birtley, Mr. Jones makes use of Exhibit Number 6 here and we see it here and questions are asked, obviously you can ask the witness questions on that clip. I mean, it's in the nature and in the substance of the cross-examination itself. But if no use has been made of, say, all the rest, then for the moment you cannot make use of that. Because I would take it that the Defence has not had time to go through all this material. And it's understandable. I mean, I don't know -- I have seen "A Cry from the Grave" before, but I've seen the video. I mean, it's -- and I have forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Agreed Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's close this. This is how we will proceed, in terms of the second option we proposed. Please do understand now that we won't have a break at 10.30. We will proceed and then I will use my judgement, obviously, as we go along, and we'll have a break, a reasonable break, later on at a reasonable time. All right. Do I have the cooperation of everyone on this? Yeah. Okay. Let's proceed. Let's bring the witness in and the two officers from the US embassy. Incidentally, while this we were discussing inside about what we had proposed to you tomorrow. You know that we had proposed to sit with you around the table tomorrow after the sitting. We've thought about it, and for the time being we've come to the conclusion we better postpone it to some other point in time. So we may come back to you when we resume in January, but for the time being we don't think that we should go ahead with what we had proposed in the first place. In the meantime, of course, we encourage the most dialogue possible between the two parts and the use of courtesy in your dealings as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, once more and welcome back. We have solved the problem that we had or so we think. And we are now able to proceed with your testimony. Our Rules require that before you start giving evidence you make a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath in your jurisdiction, to the effect that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is going to be handed now to you by Madam Usher. Please read it out and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. Could I ask the two representatives of the US State Department to identify themselves for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: I'm Clifton Johnson, and I'm the legal counsel at the US embassy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam?

utterances.speaker: MS. SCHILDGE
utterances.text: I'm Heather Schildge. I'm the deputy legal counsel at the US embassy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and welcome to this Tribunal. The rule that we have adopted here in all cases, to my knowledge, has been the following. The witness now has -- the witness now has started or is about to start giving evidence. For all intents and purposes, he is now a witness. And I understand, of course, that there may be instances where you would like to intervene, in which case you address the Trial Chamber. Draw our attention straight away to it. But there should be no tete-a-tete communication with the witness. I take it that the topics upon which cross-examination -- examination-in-chief and cross-examination are concerned have been identified, so I invite both parties not to go beyond these issues which have been authorised by the US government. Yes, having said though -- that, Mr. Jones will be examining you in examination-in-chief; that will be the direct, as you call it in your country. And Ms. Sellers, a co-national of yours, will then cross-examine you later on. Thank you. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm also a co-national of the witness's, incidentally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Good morning, Lieutenant Colonel, and apologies from me in the delay in you being brought here. You're not -- yes. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I'm okay now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're okay now. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if we could start with you giving the Court your full name.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I'm cutting on and off. Okay. There we go. My full name is Rex Edward Dudley.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If there's any problem, just let me know. And please confirm, if you can, the following details: You were born on the 1st of November, 1956, in Washington DC?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You are American by nationality?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You trained as a field artillery officer for four years and have tactical experience in artillery?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As a field artillery officer, are you familiar with the wide range of artillery weapons, their calibres, their ranges, and other characteristics?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to pause a lot for the interpretation, just so you know. Do you also have training as an airborne officer?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: With whom did you serve?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I served with the 82nd Airborne Division. I also served with southern European task force after I came out of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you trained as a tactical and operational intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were you trained in being able to analyse military situations in terms of weapons, tactics, terrain, and other key factors involving military operations?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct. That is one of my key areas of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And are you a trained military observer?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Before -- you mentioned going to Bosnia. Before being deployed to Bosnia, did you serve for 13 years as a combat intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it right you've spent 20 years in the US army?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I retired in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That was with the rank of Lieutenant Colonel?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Following your stay in Bosnia, did you write any reports, articles or manuals?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote a pamphlet that was sanctioned by US military. It was called "Tactics, Technicals and Procedures of the Warring Factions in the former Yugoslavia." And I wrote an article for a US military intelligence journal called the dagger's -- "On the Dagger's Edge." I believe that was the title. And I wrote some other various after-action report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And apart from Bosnia, were you ever posted overseas?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I served with 2nd Infantry Division in Korea. I served with various tactical and operational units in Germany. And I also served again with 2nd -- with the southern European task force in Italy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were you deployed to Bosnia and Herzegovina at the end of February 1993?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And at that time were you based in an army base, American army base, in Germany?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, in Augsburg, Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were you sent to Bosnia as the military information officer in a four-man liaison team?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you then spend some time in Sarajevo getting orientated?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: During that time did you read situation reports and otherwise inform yourself about the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. That was my initial requirement, because the United States government did not have much information at all on what was going on on the ground in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you have a communications device with you?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, we did. As part of the four-man liaison team, we brought two tactical satellite devices called TacSats.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And does that allow encrypted communication?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what was your rank at that time?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I was a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you were in Sarajevo, did you have information about the situation in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: We had minimum information because that was an area where neither the UNMOs nor the UNPROFOR had been allowed to operate very much. So there was a great big information gap.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was there anything you knew at all?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: We knew that the population was in desperate straits based on ham radio reports coming out of the enclaves and the few non-warring faction reports we got from both the UNMOs and from other observers like UNHCR reporting the bad situation there. We also know that General Morillon had just been in and come out of one area and was attempting to try to get in again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, when you were in Sarajevo, did you ever hear the name Naser Oric or Colonel Oric mentioned?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: State your question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you were in Sarajevo, did you ever hear the name Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you go to Srebrenica sometime in March in 1993?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct. I went in as part of General Morillon's team to try to enter Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what dates precisely were you in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I was in Srebrenica from March 11th to March 28th, 1993. I entered and left with General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you spent 17 days on the ground?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, was one of the reasons that you were sent to Srebrenica that you could provide secure satellite communications for General Morillon so that he could speak to his HQ using a TacSat without being intercepted?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct. That was one of the major problems with the UN at the time is they had no secure devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was another part of your mission to coordinate air-drops?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct. And that was -- my mission sort of switched. I was initially there to provide secure communications for General Morillon. And then once I was on the ground, I was also asked to coordinate all the air-drops.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in terms of your qualifications, were at least two of the reasons why you were picked for that assignment the first that you had trained in airborne operations and secondly that you knew about communications?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I think you've told us your role in Srebrenica evolved during your time there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, in your way into Srebrenica, did you have an easy entry or was your entry delayed?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: It was delayed and it was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And who delayed your entry?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: The Serb -- the Bosnian Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know why they delayed -- delayed you?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: The key-point I want to make at this time is that we were delayed because they did not want us to have access to the Muslim forces at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in terms of convoys, do you know what, if anything, was the attitude of the Serbs to UN aid convoys going into Srebrenica to provide the population with food and medicines?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: They wanted to keep them from going in to re-fit and re-equip the enemy forces, as they saw them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the first time I've spoken today, so you'll note a bit of the gravelness [sic] in my voice, but I would just ask if Defence counsel would clarify one question in relation to Bosnian Serbs, the next related to Serbs. Are we now speaking of two different groups or are we speaking of one group. Just for clarification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I can stick with Bosnian Serbs, and I can put the question again or a slightly different question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We can proceed along these lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've mentioned that the Bosnian Serbs, was the term you used, did not want you to have access and you said "to the Muslim forces at that time." Was there a distinction made between Muslim forces in Srebrenica and civilians in Srebrenica, or was all aid being blocked?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Aid was being blocked to both organisations, the Serbs -- the Bosnian Serbs, as best as I can determine, considered the entire population the enemy at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'd ask if the witness can be shown Defence Exhibit 983, D983. And just for the record, this is from the Drina Corps command, 17 of March, 1993, submitted to the regular army staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you have a look at that, Colonel, and I'll just ask you to go down to paragraph 3. It's a document, as you see it, it's submitted to the Republika Srpska army Main Staff. And it says: "Status in the responsibility area. UNPROFOR convoys passed to Sarajevo Gorazde and Tuzla but not to Srebrenica because they insisted that we let 7OT pass." Now, my first question is if I suggest that OT could refer to [B/C/S spoken], armoured transporters, would this make any sense? Would you be able to make any sense of this?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Did you say armoured transporters or supply transporters?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Armoured.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Armoured, okay. Are we talking about supplies being on these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My question is simply: Does that -- is there any comment you can offer on that sentence and in light of the date, 17th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I know that we were trying to get convoys in there and the Serbs didn't want them to go in. Did that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And if we turn to the second page, paragraph 8, and it says: "Conclusions, projections, and decisions for further combat activities." And it's the second part of that which I want to read: "I decided the following," -- by the way, this is signed by commander Colonel Milenko Zivanovic. "I decided the following, to conduct combat activities with a part of the forces to Srebrenica in order to force civilian population to surrender, break and destroy army formations of the enemy in Srebrenica. Remaining forces are to defend the existing positions not allowing the enemy to make any surprises or break through in any direction." And I just want to concentrate on those words "in order to force civilian population to surrender." Does that reflect what you told us, that in fact the Serbs regarded the whole population as the enemy, the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what -- I'm going to come back to that but I'm finished with that document for the moment. What route in fact did you take to get into to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Could I have a map, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We're going to distribute a map to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you recall, just before that's passed up, whether you were -- whether you were told that you couldn't take one route and were directed to another route?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct. General Morillon was told that the main route into Srebrenica was not available because the bridge had been destroyed. Therefore, we were diverted to a secondary route in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if you look at the map which is being placed on the ELMO to your right and if you mark preferably with a highlighter the road that you took.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I will trace it first with a pen and then I will highlight it. From Bratunac we were diverted from the main redball road into Srebrenica to a secondary road, which I'm going to trace first with the pointer and then I'll highlight with a pen. We came up this narrow winding road that was unpaved through the snow and where we were hit the redball and then were able to come into Srebrenica. I will now highlight it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you encounter any mines on the way in?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. We encountered one mine that blew up a supply truck, the only supply truck that we had been able to bring in because the Serbs didn't allow the other ones to come in. And the mine was approximately right there where my pen is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you mark that with an X, please?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I would be glad to. I've got one right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you also just sign the map, so we don't forget, and then ask for an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're initials, please, next to that "X" that you marked on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So this map will become Defence Exhibit D99?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D996, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So that road, in fact, was mined?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when, in fact, did you arrive in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: We arrived that night after nightfall, and I'm going to say approximately 8.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you arrive in a vehicle or on foot?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: We -- I arrived in an armoured personnel carrier after the vehicle I was riding in was blocked by the destroyed vehicle. So my communications -- I had to walk through the snow for approximately six kilometres. We were picked up by a Belgian Jeep, delivered to an armoured personnel carrier -- the one armoured personnel carrier in the convoy. We got inside of that, and then proceeded on to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So did you, in fact, walk on foot on a mined road?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were you with anyone else when you were walking along?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I had my communications sergeant with me and I had him stay approximately 100 metres behind me in case I stepped on a mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How did you ensure that you didn't step on a mine?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: There was no way that I could ensure it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you encounter anyone that evening who might be described as a fighter when you arrived in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Once we caught up with General Morillon and the M-113 armoured personnel carrier, we proceeded a little way and these shadowy figures came out of the forest, walked our route, and then several of them mounted on to the M-113, and we found out that they were local fighters from Srebrenica. And they proceeded to escort us into the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how did they appear?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: They were a rather motley group. They were armed with various light arms, mostly hunting rifles. They were poorly clothed. They had a wide variety of clothing on, basically anything to keep them warm. Same thing with their shoes. And they did not -- they appeared more like partisans than anything else, not a trained fighting force.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what were your first impressions of Srebrenica when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Horrendous.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What was the situation like in terms of any refugees?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: As soon as we drove into the main town, we pulled up to the PTT building, their post telegraph and telephone building. And we were ushered into the building, but I could -- it was already dark. And there were refugee families scattered throughout the town area blocking the road on both sides of the road, huddled around fires trying to stay warm. The key thing that I noticed, it was -- there was no light because there was no electricity, and there was -- I mean, just several hundred refugees just in that one little area next to the post telegraph and telephone building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were you able to estimate during your stay in Srebrenica how many refugees there were in the enclave roughly at that time?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I went through with -- I have to remember his name now. The UNHCR --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, please don't mention the name of UNHCR representative. If you need to, then we'll go into private session. But for the moment you can see "UNHCR representative."

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Fine. I went in with a UNHCR representative, and we went from building to building, up and down Srebrenica counting windows and estimating approximately how many people were actually in Srebrenica itself. We came to the conclusion it was approximately 30.000 people in a town that was only designed to hold about 10.000. Not to mention all the refugees who were in the immediate outlying areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, Mr. Jones. Ms. Sellers, do you require the name of this UNHCR representative that the witness spoke to on that occasion? Because if you do, we'll go into private session, we'll have his name, and then continue in open session afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll inform of course the Defence and Trial Chamber that we're aware of the name, and we would agree that the name need not be mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So let's go ahead then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So 30.000 people in the town, not to mention all the refugees who were in the immediate outlying areas, you said. So overall how many people in the pocket?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: We estimated when we did the first head count there were between 50 and 60.000 people inside the pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now we're going to see a short clip of a video; it's D700. And as we go along, if you want to make a comment, then just start speaking, and we'll stop the video, and you can make your comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: "The news seems to keep getting worse out of Bosnia, numbing us with its relentlessness. But we get shocked anew each time we see the pictures, and today for the first time we get a glimpse of life in Eastern Bosnia, the isolated mountainous area where thousands of Muslim refugees are slowly starving as the United States searches for ways to get food to the people without getting involved in their war. When the Serbs refused to let United Nations relief trucks travel into the Muslim areas of Eastern Bosnia, the US started dropping supplies from the sky. For weeks now the US air force, flying out of Weinheim air force base, has carried tonnes of food and medicine to the people of Bosnia while the American people wonder whether the supplies are getting through, whether they're doing any good, and whether any of the factions have devised a way to use food as a weapon. We have seen the eery pictures of American planes dropping their bulky beacons of survival. Tonight we see where the parcels land and surprisingly, the first sign of an American military man on the ground in Eastern Bosnia. He's witnessed the impact of the air-drops. These scenes come to us from the town of Srebrenica, a place almost impossible to get to. ABC's Tony Birtley finally managed it last week in what can only be described as a heroic effort to let us see what is happening in Srebrenica. Tony travelled by foot and by horseback to get into the isolated area. Since he arrived, he's run out of food and been injured by Serbian fire. But still, he smuggled out the story."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stop the tape. I'd just like to state that that is exactly what I saw when I drove in on the M-113. And those little family groups huddling fires has been burned in my memory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "... the hillsides to wait for what they call the planes from God. After 11 months under Serbian siege, the US air-drops of humanitarian aid are their only life-line. In the dead of night, they make their way to the place where the prepared meals have landed, most often on steep-sided hills where people have to crawl up on their hands and knees. For some like this lady, it's too much. She collapsed from exhaustion. But the shape of a US parachute hanging in the trees showing the drop spot. Gun-fire echos around as the army try to control the people and the supplies. "I found this about 600 yards uphill. I don't know what it is. It could be medicine or something."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, I just want to ask you Colonel Dudley, do you recognise where those scenes were?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do. They were just to the south of Srebrenica and very close to the fortress. Let me show it on the map. Here is Srebrenica itself. This was a Turkish fortress that was located approximately here, and the air-drops were being dropped just south of them on a sloping hill. One of the key problems with that location was that all the refugees knew that that was where the air-drop was and so they could congregate there. And as soon as they heard the airplanes coming, they would get out on to the drop zone itself. And when you drop a pallet full of food or other heavy stuff with parachutes, they fall rather rapidly, and if people get under them or close to them, they get crushed or rather seriously injured. The other problem is the local authorities had totally lost control of this huge refugee population. So it was every person for themselves. They act like wolves, fighting over the contents. And the first night that I witnessed this I believe that at three people were killed by the pallets and/or by gun-fire or by being stabbed. It was a very vicious environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll continue with the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness points to a section below Srebrenica at 30 minutes, approximately once centimetre down from the name. Could you mark it with an "L" -- "LP," that's landing place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that location also known as the Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I can't say that for sure. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. We'll continue on with the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: "The lucky ones clutch their treasured packet of 12 meals and head home. But in the morning the empty packets lying on the mountain track showing that some were so desperate for food they couldn't wait. "American planes have successfully air dropped aid into this area for the last five nights running. The villagers say they received only one prepared lunch packet. The rest has been taken by the army. "Most people have been eating only bread made from hay and corn for the last two months. That has finished. They now make it from the flower from a hazelnut tree. The father of this family demonstrates how much weight he has lost in the last 11 months. It is not a famine situation here but it can be best described as slow starvation. "This is what I eat. This is what we eat. "We've got nothing to eat. We're starving to death. "We're practically naked and barefoot. Look at us, we're all in rags. We haven't had anything to eat. "The air-drops have worked, but the people need land convoys which are continually being blocked by the Serbs. "So far we have been right on the money. I see [indiscernible] packages everywhere. I see people carrying MRE supplies. However, we need to change our distribution now to flour, sugar, oil, and other basic necessities. These are very hungry people, and they need basic supplies, not high-calorie items like MRE. Right now we have done the bare minimum to keep them from starving and from dying. However, we need to do a lot more. "General Philippe Morillon, the commander of the UN forces in Bosnia, visited the town. He told the authorities that he would open up road corridors to get food in and ordered the placement of military observers in the town which he hopes will deter shelling that locals" --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, I meant to stop a second ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you recognise the UNPROFOR officer who was unloading?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. He was a Canadian staff sergeant who was in charge of that infantry squad who accompanied us into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recall his name?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No. But if you can mention it, I know I would know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if I'm allowed to lead that name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would have no objection from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Ms. Sellers. Yes, Mr. Jones, you may lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would it be Sergeant Morrison?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct. That is exactly who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we will keep playing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: "...to get food in and order the placement of military observers in the town that he hopes will deter shelling that locals say come to [indiscernible] nearby Drina River in Serbia. But the Serbs have so far failed to give their agreement to the General's plans. "That's when General Morillon tried to leave. Hundreds of refugees, many of them recent arrivals from Konjevic Polje blocked his way."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I just want to ask you: Do you recognise the man on the right, first of all?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. That is his Macedonian interpreter/body-guard, and he was serving in the French Foreign Legion at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. Just -- it was the man on the right who I was starting with and then the man on the left. If you can talk us through that.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Oh. This is General Morillon, and this is his Macedonian body-guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Standing to his right but to our left?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct. The two men with the blue berets on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: "Peace and food and believed that if the UN commander left, the Serbs would start shelling. "The tanks are above waiting to attack. If you will leave, they will come and attack us. "I heard the news that General Mladic will attack Srebrenica. We just want bread. We want the blue helmets to protect us. "They kept their vigil all night around fires, and in the end General Morillon decided to stay until a cease-fire takes effect and the Serbs allow UN helicopters to fly into Srebrenica. "I discovered on arriving here that the situation was lost and I feared myself. And I understood the real fear, anguish, panic, of this population. And I wondered, too, that their desire for me to stay here was probably the best solution in order to help them to survive. "The refugee problem is so acute that people are being forced to live in" --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think actually in the interests of time we can probably stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is there anything -- you've seen this video. Is there anything in terms of depicting the situation which you would quibble with or as it an accurate reflection?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That was a very accurate video, particularly the mobs of refugees that were in and around Srebrenica. And I think the video showed how desperate the people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the video, we saw there, if I may call it a crisis situation, involving Morillon being held in the town against his will. Is that something which you know about?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, it was. When we first got into Srebrenica, we were all put into the PTT building at night, and we were not allowed to leave. We moved up to the second floor, and we were put into -- like in a dark, dank large room, and we were not allowed to leave it. General Morillon attempted to sneak out during the night to get out of town, and he came back in when he was not able to liaison with who he was looking to liaison with. The rest of us stayed up on the second floor. And again, those who were blocking us in were not the authorities/soldiers. It was all the refugees who had surrendered us and would not allow us to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did they say why they didn't want you to leave?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, it was very obvious. If General Morillon left, then the Serbs would continue the shelling, and they were afraid they were all going to get killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did this action by the refugees, did it appear to you to be organised or spontaneous?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: It was very much spontaneous. There was no leadership around to deal with that spontaneous type of environment. These were just a bunch of desperate women with their families. And it's actually interesting. The women were the ones who were leading this protest, where usually in an organised demonstration if you see man out there leading the chant, and everybody everyone is in a semi-organised environment. This place was -- it was totally spontaneous. And they would -- they stayed there all night, literally sleeping out in the snow and cold in order to block us in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we have seen the video and a description of the state of the people in terms of lack of food and shelter. Do you know why they were in that situation?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: They had been driven out of their village areas around the perimeter of Srebrenica, slowly forced in as the Serb military was peeling the onion or tightening the noose around the enclave of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, during your time in Srebrenica, did you also try to find out who the players were in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. In order to do my job, particularly with coordinating the air-drops, I needed to know who the key civil and military leadership was in order to coordinate security and distribution of the supplies that were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I think the transcript doesn't reflect -- you said the key civil and military leadership. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that something you worked on a great deal?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is there any aspect of your training or background which equipped you for that sort of analysis?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I had detailed training in establishing who the key leadership was, what the terrain is like, what the weather is like, et cetera, so that the leadership can make good decisions on the battlefield. So that was one of my key jobs to decide who the key players were in order to do the military mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And during your time in Srebrenica, did you reach any firm conclusions about that?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No. Who the actual leadership was within Srebrenica and who could actually accomplish requirements always remained fuzzy for me. I was never able to link up who was actually the key players in the Presidency or in the -- if you can call it, the military leadership and how they crossed over. Those lines were very, very fuzzy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you conclude that there was one player or multiple player or?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: There were multiple players in this environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you detect or find out about any clear delineation of duties and responsibilities among those players?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I was able to get some vague ideas of first who was able to help me get my mission accomplished, and this is who I focussed on. And then the second as far as delineation of power groups, there was a War Presidency group, there was Naser, who was in charge of the semi-autonomous military group, and then there was the police in blue uniforms who were basically in charge of taking care of the internal security and control of the Srebrenica town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So the police were basically in charge of internal security in the town of Srebrenica itself, in terms of -- in charge of law and order, would you say?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I would say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to come to each of those players one at a time. But my question was whether you detected a clear delineation of duties?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No, I did not. That was one of the things I noticed was that the different groups seemed to cross over and back again based on the situation on the ground and what was going on. I would like to state here also that everybody in the pocket, particularly the leadership, had almost a lethargic attitude to the situation because they were literally worn out, and they just felt that they couldn't accomplish much anymore. There was an exhausted look on everybody's face.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a War Presidency. Did you meet members of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. While I was in Srebrenica, I didn't know who was what within the War Presidency, but I did notice that -- I got introduced to some key people like the mayor and one member, I remember, with a dark beard who was a member of the War Presidency and I had dinner at his apartment house, but I never had much interaction with these people. I attempted to get them to assist me, but none of them really stepped forward and said, I will help you do your job.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We're going to play a bit of a video. It's P318. And we're going to play from 04.07 to 04.14. Just while that's being brought up: Was the War Presidency and these members, were they among the players whom you identified?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you referred to the local authorities, does that describe the War Presidency and the mayor and those players?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Let me state that one again. When I say the players or the leadership within the Srebrenica pocket, there was a War Presidency, there was the semi-autonomous military groups that had a leader in the sense of Naser - he was just mentioned as the leader of that group - and then there was the police, who seemed to be a separate organisation unto themselves. And the hospital -- there was a hospital group, but again, they focussed on the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. As I say, I'm going to come to these one at a time. So if we just, first of all, look at this -- the video, P318. Do you recognise that person?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I have to go to the video. One moment. Yes, that's the mayor of the city of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't know if for the record we can give a time. Yes, 04.07.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that, Mr. Jones. It is indeed 04.07.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could now go to 4.22. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone in that frame?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I'm attempting to get the picture -- oh, here we go. Yes, the man on the left with the beard was a member of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was he the one who you had dinner with or was that someone else?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That was the one I had dinner with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown D872.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I simply want to ask you this: In terms of the War Presidency and the mayor, how were they coping with the refugee and humanitarian situation?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: They were not. They were overwhelmed by the task, and they appeared to have given up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if you'll look at the next photo which is being placed on the monitor, as for the man in the middle, do you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, that was the same man I had dinner with and he was a member of the War Presidency. I don't know his name, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the person on the left and the person on the right, if you can help us with that?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: The person on the left is myself, with the sunglasses on, and the person on the right is Senad, who initially became my body-guard/keeper and later my interpreter. Those roles switched as he became comfortable with me doing my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, in that situation, right there in that scene, do you recall that scene?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I was trying to find out what the actual number of refugees were -- excuse me, wounded people that we needed to evacuate. And we had a very difficult conversation. We had a lot of people around us. Again, this is by the PTT building, and the crowds were everywhere. So I was having Senad, on the right, translate my English into Bosniak to the War Presidency individual. And we were not clear in our communication at all. So later on I had the three of us move off to a quiet location where we could sit down and I could actually get the facts with how many translations we needed to make it happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Now, let me take this step by step. Firstly before I come to Senad, the person in the middle who you've mentioned, did many people at the time in Srebrenica have beards like his?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Almost all the men who could grow a beard had a beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was it easy to distinguish among them?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No, it was not -- let me take that back. If they had striking features or I had met them personally and had dealt with them, then, yes, I could pick them out from a crowd. Otherwise, it was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now going to Senad, do you remember his last name?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Not off the top of my head, but if I saw it in writing or it was told to me I would be able to remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. We can leave that for now. So you said he was in interpreting. In what language or languages did he interpret?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: He spoke mediocre English and fairly good German because he lived in Germany for a while, and of course he spoke fluent Bosniak -- Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were you speaking some German or how was your German?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: My German was horrible. His English was pretty bad, too. And so we would communicate back and forth in broken English and broken German.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So it was actually very difficult, as you've told us, to communicate sometimes?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct. And we had to go over very simple issues multiple times in order to make sure that we had communicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did Senad interpret between you and other locals while you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, he did. After he -- we established a working relationship, he was the key person I used to coordinate air-drop security and other things that I was trying to accomplish in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in fact, this dinner that you went to with the bearded man in the middle, was Senad interpreting for you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
