utterances.text: To be honest, I cannot honestly recollect, but I'm almost positive that he was the one who was there because nobody else could speak passable English that I worked with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know how long he had been in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: He had gotten there just prior to me arriving. I was going to say January/early February time frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know where he came from and with whom he travelled?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: He came out of Tuzla with a small group of fighting men, as he told me. They had infiltrated through the Serb lines, and they had brought a German reporter/photographer with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you remember his name, the name of the photographer?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: He was a tall, lanky guy. Again, I'm sorry for my name recall right now, but if you give me the name I know I would know it. He was the only German photographer in Srebrenica at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. I don't think there's anything in dispute who that was. Was there anything about Senad's appearance that indicated he was a recent arrival in the pocket?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Well, there were multiple indicators. If you take a look at the photograph itself, you'll notice the difference between the War Presidency individual with his shrunken cheeks, meaning he hadn't eaten very well for a long time, and a lot of the other people had the same appearance. Senad on the other side had relatively fleshy cheeks, had a light beard, was relatively well-cleaned. There were no bags under his eyes because they were still relatively fresh. He was in a complete uniform, which was very fascinating to me. He has good combat boots on. He had a good functional uniform. He had a full military vest that I believe came out of either China or North Korea with banana AK clips in it. He had a AK assault rifle that was also in very good condition, which was also a rarity inside Srebrenica. Very few men actually carried assault rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And aside from assault rifle, having a clean uniform and combat boots, et cetera, was that usual or unusual in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That was extremely unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you remember roughly how old he was?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: He was 20 years old at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you know if he's still living?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No. I had been informed later on -- well, I received a postcard from him from Tuzla stating that he was alive. And then later on I was informed that he had been killed in an automobile accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Apart from Senad, was there anyone else, any local, who accompanied you a lot in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. There was a local one-armed police officer by the name of Zele. And I will remember -- his first name was -- give me two minutes. He had been a drummer in a band. He had lost his arm -- right arm I believe, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Don't worry about the name. We can come back to that.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Djozic. And then the first name is going to come to me in just a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now you've told us he was a police officer?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that civilian police or military police?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: At the time I didn't know what he was. All the police were the same to me. And I believe he was a civil policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did he mention any sort of title that he had?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No subtitle. He was just -- he was introduced to me as a police chief, and there was no delineation made at the time of whether he was the chief of police or just a subordinate chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in fact, in terms of titles which you heard when you were in Srebrenica, were there official titles which remained fixed or were they shifting?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: In a few cases they remained fixed, like, you know, a member of the War Presidency mayor. But other titles would sort of shift or evolve. People seemed to give themselves self-promotions at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did Zele perform any sort of liaison function for you?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Zele was very important to me because the civil police were one of the few functional groups there that were organised and seemed to have a good cohesive team. And so I used Zele to assist me in securing drop zones that were close to the town, and I can give one instance of that where he was vital for us. And then he also helped me to secure the soccer stadium when we were doing the evacuation of the wounded. There was no other force there that I could depend on of locals who were dependable. If I would give them a mission, they would fail miserably.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did Zele ever point out to you where he worked?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what was that building, as far as you --

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: It was the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit P419, please. Actually, may I look at the photographs because I see there's a whole number and I can show which one ... it's ERN 036617724.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you can have a look and see whether that's the building or not that was pointed out to you.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were you ever told whether there was a prison there?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Zele mentioned once when we were coming back through Srebrenica, and he just casually pointed out, That's where I worked, and he mentioned that he had had to confine a young Bosnian soldier in there who had committed some sort of a crime. So, yes, there was some port of a prison in that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now -- that's fine for those photographs. Thank you. Now -- so now you've mentioned in addition to some -- the mayor and this other member of the War Presidency, Senad and Zele, were they among the players whom you identified?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I would say yes because they were competent enough or had enough connections to get things accomplished.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And -- yes. And you said that Zele was in the civil police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask that you be shown D871 and see if you can find his name on this list. For the record, this is Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sarajevo Ministry of the Interior, Tuzla Security Services Centre, Srebrenica public security station, list of the members of the Srebrenica SJB, dated 25 April 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you could turn to the second page, look down that list. Do you see a familiar name?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Oh, there we go. Yes, his first name is Elvir Djozic. And I see here he was a clerical officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that's who you recall as Zele?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct. He was the only one-armed man in the town. He was very recognisable.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, as far as this civilian police is concerned, did you gain any understanding during your time in Srebrenica as to where they were operating, within which geographical area?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: The civil police operated inside Srebrenica itself, as far as I saw. They were a presence always in front of the PTT building helping us with security. And whenever we had large crowds or other issues showing up, those were the people who I always saw. I didn't see who I would call the fighters, the village folk who picked up arms doing any type of missions inside Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. So when you say "inside Srebrenica itself," you mean the town, the town of Srebrenica itself?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I think you mentioned a hospital in Srebrenica. Did you go there when you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I went there multiple times to deliver medical supplies. I also went inside the building when the Canadians had been wounded during our attempt to do an air evacuation of the wounded Bosnians, and I also went in there and took a tour of the hospital once.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was it a proper hospital building?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No -- well, it was a shell of a hospital building, but they had none of the equipment or other facilities that you would expect in a normal hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you liaise with the hospital and with UNHCR regarding medical supplies to be dropped?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct. That was one of my key goals is get the right supplies on the air-drops so to help re-fit or re-equip the hospitals with the basic necessities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And so were the hospital staff, again, among the players whom you identified?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've told us there were multiple players in Srebrenica. In terms of the military, was there one player in Srebrenica or many?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: There were many players in the military. Would you like me to elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: The players in Srebrenica evolved, as best as I could determine. When the war started, the outlying villages had a chief or popular leader, and they basically picked up arms to defend themselves when the violence started. As these villages collapsed, they would sort of group together and move on to the next village. And so they would basically be local fighters, through necessity, that had banded together around a chief, and those were the small groups that I saw as fighters. And they would number between 20 and a hundred people roughly in these village groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Naser Oric earlier. As far as you know, did he have his own group?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I can't confirm or deny that. I never saw him with his group or heard that he had his own individual group.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You referred to -- you used the term, I think, "semi-autonomous." Can you explain what that means, please?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Certainly. These groups were not a trained military force, and they were still very distrustful of even people from other villages. They did not seem to work well in an organised fashion. They didn't have the military training, communications, or other intelligence to plan out a cohesive, organised, combined-arms operation. They basically worked in small strike forces, going out and doing raids or securing a part of the perimeter of Srebrenica, but that was about all they seemed to be capable of doing. Did that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to break it down into smaller -- smaller parts. You referred to this organisation on a village level, and you've mentioned the size of fighting units, I think you said between 20 and a hundred people. So these groups which were semi-autonomous, is that what you were --

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yeah, that's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you speak to people about the military situation in making these observations?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Because one of my key tasks because of the air-drop operation was to see how well the front lines were holding because I didn't want to put an air-drop too close to the front lines. So I was figuring out how well these -- the defence of the perimeter was going to last, and there was a concern that it was going to collapse at any time while I was there on numerous occasions. Therefore, I focussed on observing exactly how these military groups interacted, how they departed, how they came back. And what I would see is that they would be defending a specific part of the perimeter, using an area that they were personally familiar with, and they would move out for 24 to 72 hours, and then they would return and another group would go out there and replace them. They had no formal communications except for a siren in town that I heard once or twice sound off to assemble groups for mass mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Can I stop you there. You're giving a lengthy answer, and I want to -- like I said, I want to take it bit by bit.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You're anticipating matters which I'm going to come to. So if we just -- if you can just give very short -- if possible, short answers to the next few questions. Firstly, these groups organised on a village level, were they conducting combined operations from what you could observe?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No, they were not. They were conducting light infantry operations on a small scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, do you know if these fighters were living in barracks or with their families?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: They were living with their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did that have any effect on their way of fighting?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, it did because they were very concerned about their families, and a lot of them didn't want to leave their families to go up to the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, to your knowledge were the refugees among the fighters? If that wasn't clear, let me put it again because it was meant to be a simple question. Among the fighters, were there people who were refugees?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Well, in the sense that some of the fighters' families had been chased into Srebrenica also, yes, some of the fighters were -- also be classified as refugees from the villages that had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did that fact affect the way of fighting in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, it did because the fighters had a dual responsibility, as one is to take care of the family but also try to keep the pocket from collapsing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And so that might be described as dual loyalties?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what was, in fact, happening to the pocket while you were there?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: It was continually shrinking from both the south and from the north. The Serbs had a pincher movement that was, again, slowly collapsing the pockets, like -- peeling an onion is the best description I can give.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I want to refer the witness to D199 I think it is. It's the book "War Hospital," and I'm going to read a passage from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But it's probably best if you have that in front of you. Thanks. It's pages 154 to 155. And It's the following passage, it's the bottom, the last paragraph, and it's referring to -- to yourself. "Constantly shadowed by two Bosnian minders, he has also mapped the perimeter of the enclave and attempted to understand what the Muslims and Serbs in this part of Bosnia are fighting about." Now, firstly, who are those two minders?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't see the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's the last paragraph on page 154.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Wrong page. Start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yeah. You'll see around the middle of the page it refers to you, and then further down, the last paragraph: "Constantly shadowed by two Bosnian minders, he had also mapped the perimeter of the enclave and attempted to understand what the Muslims and the Serbs in this part of Bosnia are fighting about." Who would be the two minders?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That would be Senad and Zele.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's correct now. It continues: "He has concluded that the valley of Srebrenica is evidently defendable and identified positions from which it can be protected. He explained to some key Bosnian soldiers that they should dig up the roads and block the trails leading in to the town and set up defence in depth forward positions with multiple fall-back positions. This way, the light infantry could fight off an armoured Serb attack. When the Bosnians argued they couldn't put it off, he advised them to get out. The place is the Alamo [phoen], he thinks. It isn't going to last." Now, firstly, do you recall that exchange with Senad and Zele?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is that passage an accurate reflection of your thoughts in the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Apologies, this monitor has a tendency to shut itself off every 30 minutes, which isn't very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, can you explain a bit more what you were proposing there in that passage?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The Bosniaks inside Srebrenica were only doing light infantry raids whilst there and/or manning the perimeter. They were not providing themselves with any active defensive positions from which to fight from. And therefore, the hardball road leading from both the north and the south into Srebrenica were basically undefended by any type of obstacles. Having been trained as an airborne officer and anti-armour defence, I understood the importance of blocking avenues of approach to armoured vehicles. And the key thing you do is block off any hardball roads that can support an armoured defensive, which was both sides of the valley. The Bosnians had done nothing to do that. Therefore, they remained very vulnerable to high-speed, armoured approaches or attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the interpretation. Now, you as a trained military officer were there advising them on what they might do to prevent that happening, and they told you they couldn't do it?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct. There didn't seem to be the organisation or the will to carry out an active defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, we'll have a break at noon, so plan accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, were there many trained military men among the Srebrenica fighters?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what was the general level of education or culture of the people you met in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: This is not meant to be an insult to the people of Srebrenica, but I found that a lot of the people were not much smarter than the animals that they owned. I could -- they had a very low educational level, and they had no concept of what I would call complex operations or how to carry them off.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And again, I don't know if you still have D199 in front of you, "War Hospital," but if not there's a passage at page 94 and I can just read it -- you do have it, yes. Okay. And this refers to a trip made by a member of an NGO to the hospital describing the hospital. And he says -- it's the bottom of the second paragraph: "A patient's broken femur wasn't even stretched into traction, and the most vivid image in his mind is of a crying little girl with her pathetic home-made splint. They could have devised something better for her, he thinks. All of it lends the impression of a medical team so overwhelmed by the situation that they are no longer able to see what they can achieve. They have all but given up." I'm just wondering whether that in any way is also -- was reflected among the fighters to whom you spoke, that attitude?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that the fighters were very demoralised at this time because they were consistently losing ground and the Serbs seemed to be gaining momentum, and there just seemed to be an apathy or lack of will to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what you proposed about these blocking manoeuvres was actually a matter of survival, was it not?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And they weren't able to muster the organisation to do it?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we have a second part of a video -- in fact, I think we -- I'm sorry, we have a portion of a video. It's D700. It's another portion, and I think we have time before the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When I say "noon," it could be plus or minus a little bit, Mr. Jones, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll time it accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: "... resigned to defeat. You've got to be resigned to injury, and also you've got to be resigned to death. It's a totally mismatch. If it was a big fight ... equivalent of Mike Tyson fighting some 15-year-old with both arms tied behind his back. They don't have weapons to complete on a level footing with what the Serbs have got. They have 1948, 1950 weapons. They have Kalashnikovs if they're lucky. They've got a couple of tanks that they captured from the Serbs, but they can't fire them because they ran out of ammunition a long, long time ago."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, it was just that portion we want to show you. First, did you recognise the person speaking at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That was Tony Birtley.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you meet him in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. And we had several deep conversations and he seemed to like to follow me around because I was an event that he could film.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we saw scenes there of people walking along with weapons. Is that how you recall Srebrenica's fighters when you --

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That was a very typical group of fighters right there, the age, the dress, and the equipment they carried. Actually, those were better-armed than most of them I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, when you were in Srebrenica, did you try to establish what sort of structure, if any, the fighters had?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Because I was again very interested in how well they were going to be able to hold the perimeter knowing and seeing what the Serb army also had at the -- available to them to conduct the operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you analyse that from a tactical perspective?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And that was my major concern is: Were these people going to be able to hold this terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, how could you categorise Srebrenica's fighters? Were they like regular soldiers, reserve soldiers, or some other type of fighters?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I looked at soldiers from three different levels. You have the professional military person who's been trained, equipped, and prepared for a specific operation. They're well-disciplined, and they know what they're about. You have reserve soldiers who, with a little bit of training, can usually be brought up to standard for a specific operation, but you can't task them with complex operations because they just haven't had the years of experience doing it again and again and again. The last group is a citizen soldier who takes up arms for various reasons but he might have had like a year's worth of conscript training, like the JNA army did, but they haven't trained for years. They're out of shape, poorly equipped, poorly armed, poorly disciplined, and they're doing it out of necessity, not because they are an organised force.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now turning to Srebrenica, which was it?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Okay. In Srebrenica it was obvious. These people were mostly out of the villages, and they had grouped together for mutual defence, so they were that last category. Can I make one more note here? I didn't meet a single trained professional military man the entire time I was in Srebrenica that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And now might have touched on this already, but what sort of weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Well, first off, they were poorly equipped for the combat that they were engaged in for the most part. They had individual hunting rifles and/or shotguns, which seemed to be the predominant weapon. I saw everything from a little spider machine-gun with a 22-calibre bullet, which is totally useless in that environment, to a few good recent Kalashnikovs. But again, the great majority of weapons were individually owned weapons, old hunting rifles, shotguns, that type of stuff very few machine-guns, and one of the things they seemed to be lacking was ammunition, particularly for their automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did they have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Not that you could call it a uniform, no. They were wearing anything that was going to work in the environment in which they were operating, whatever they could scrounge together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did they wear signs of ranks?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: None that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I think it might just be useful at this stage to go briefly to Exhibit P -- one moment, please. P318, which we saw earlier. And I'd like to go to 4.33, 04.33 -- sorry, it's a video clip. Now, firstly, do you ever recall seeing that man when you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No. I do not remember seeing him while I was in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to ask you about the uniform which that person is wearing. Have a very careful look and tell us if there's anything about it which you can help us with.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: There is one key item that I see on this uniform that I find very interesting because he's wearing the exact same type of weapon carrier that I was wearing. And that's that strap that goes over his shoulders and comes down and attaches to a web belt which we carry ammunition and other items in. This is very unusual because it looks like it's US military equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that or is that not a uniform of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: The one that he's actually wearing, it doesn't look like a -- I can't see the camouflage, but it doesn't look like Bosnian army camouflage. It looks almost like US military camouflage. But I can't tell from this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you were in Srebrenica, did you see people wearing different types of camouflage?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I didn't see much camouflage at all, to be perfectly honest, because they didn't have it available to them. I saw some synthetic pants that were camouflage and camouflage jackets. But I saw mostly older dark green or other old, worn-out type uniforms. But I didn't see a whole lot of camouflage when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think I prefer to have the break at this stage, if that's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Jones. We'll have a 30-minute break, which means we'll resume at 20 minutes past 12.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Dudley, are you familiar with the term "C3I"?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I am. It's a standard American military term.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I should say -- we've had complaints from the stenographer and the interpreters about not pausing. So if I'm pausing before the next question, that's what that's about. What does it stand for, that term?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: C3I means command, control, communications and intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And does that refer, in essence, to what's required for effective command and control?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That's exactly right. All four of those elements have to be present in order for a military commander to conduct complex operations on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And from what you observed of the fighters in Srebrenica, did they have what was required for command and control?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I want to take it -- well, first of all, based on your observations, did the conditions exist for a commander to be effective on the ground?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: In the situation in Srebrenica, I don't think any commander who walked into that environment would be very successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you make that observation in terms, as well, of the training, equipment, and conditions necessary to organise military operations into planned, sustained operations?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Not only was the equipment missing, but a key component, communications, was also missing from that enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, how important are good communications to command and control?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Very, particularly for more complex combat operations. I would like to make a point here is that the terrain of Srebrenica was very broken up, very hilly, very compartmentalised, and therefore being able to communicate with subordinate leaders or commanders on the ground, you would have to have good, solid communications between a commander -- subordinate commanders to make sure that the forces stay coordinated in a well-involved complex plan that people knew so they would deal with various contingencies they would run into in their area of operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And so as part of that, is it necessary to have rapid or indeed instantaneous communications?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, particularly if you're dealing with a -- if you were doing a defence and you're dealing with the enemy leading an attack, you would have to be able to react quickly to deal with various contingencies that might arise. So communications would be vital to coordinate your forces, operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, do you know how the people of Srebrenica communicated with the outside world when you were there?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. They had a ham radio station located in the PT building up on the second floor facing towards the south. That was their primary means of communication with the outside world.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know who operated the ham radio?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. There were two twins who basically owned that ham radio station, and they traded off operating it. But every time I saw them, they were almost always together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if the witness could be shown D785.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recognise those men?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the two twins I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was that the equipment which they operated or was there something else?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That was the equipment they operated with. You notice that they have a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we better put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had this device which of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- was for Morse code. And then they had the small ham radio station that was operated -- was electrically generated from the stream outside. It was a relatively simple device.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask if the witness could be shown - it will be on the monitor - Exhibit C2; it's actually a Court exhibit. There are a number of photographs, and we have two which should appear on the monitor under computer evidence, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, first of all, do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, that is the PTT building within Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can you recall where these twins were operating?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. This is the main entrance -- I'm sorry, I don't have another picture to point at. You can see the main entrance is that oval hall on the bottom left of the screen. They were right above that. You follow the stairwell up the stairs and they were off to the left on the south end of the building in a relatively small room. I believe there was a wood-burning stove in that room, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And there's another picture which I believe is a side-view.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, there we go. That's the side that the twins were on, and again they were up on the second floor, last window to the left of the picture. And again, their electricity came from the stream that ran right behind the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were they dressed, just as we saw in the picture there, in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I particularly remember the one twin wearing that grey, heavy jacket all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was there any guard on duty barring entry to that room?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Not that I remember. We on the staff had relatively free access. The only guards I remember were the civilian police who were on the outside of the PTT building, and they were supporting our Canadian guards, who were remaining security for ourselves inside that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the radio equipment that they had, was it sophisticated or unsophisticated?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: It was very basic ham radio equipment. I don't remember it being very sophisticated at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if someone were to say the following about that ham radio, would it be correct, and if you can help us with this, we would appreciate it. If someone said that it was a big, solid, commercial piece of machinery, two by three metres long by three metres high, with many switches and knobs, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That's a false statement. Because you can see in the picture exactly what it consisted of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know in the PTT building was there anything which might approximate to that, what I've just described?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. In an adjacent room, almost in the centre of the second floor, there were two banks of inoperatable telecommunications equipment. Basically it looked like a telephone switchboard type of setup, and there were lots of loose wires and things hanging off of it, and it was non-functional.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So were these twins sitting by this machinery which you've just described or by the ham radio that we saw a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: They were sitting by the ham radio station that was in the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How much time did you spend in the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: To be honest, for the first couple of days I spent a lot of time there until I got freedom of movement, and then when I came back to the PTT building to sleep, which I usually did in the afternoon before night operations started. So once things got exciting and I got freedom of movement, not that much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You're familiar with its layout?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Very familiar with its layout.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you see any maps in the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. There was one map up on the second floor in a conference room that was adjacent to where the ham operators were working out of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was that old or new?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: It was an old, outdated map, and I believe it was of most of Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And from what you could see, was it being used for any purpose to mark front lines or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No, it was not. It was actually a little bit worn-out looking. It also looked very outdated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And apart from the ham radio, what sort of communications did you see in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: In that same room where I mentioned the ham radio operators, or in the adjacent room, I can't quite remember which, they had torn-apart Motorola radios that they were trying to piece together to form at least one functional set. I don't know how successful they were in doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you're familiar with communications. What's the range of one of those Motorolas, assuming that they can be made functional?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Those Motorolas would have very short line-of-sight communication, maybe from one end of Srebrenica to the other, but much further and definitely not through a hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you had your TacSat with you as you described. At the time was that a sophisticated piece of machinery?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: At the time, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you have easy communications with your TacSat when you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No -- let me rephrase that. Initially, no, because we were in a steep, mountain valley, which is where Srebrenica was located. And we had to have line of sight with the satellite we were using to send our communications through. And so we had a very short period of time, particularly at night, when we could access that satellite, otherwise we had to get out of that valley and set up on a ridge-line outside of the town where we could have a much broader location.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, while we're discussing command and control issues, did the refugee situation have an impact on the potential for command and control?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Most definitely. The refugees were blocking -- they were taking up logistics supplies, namely food. They were taking up medicine, what little bit was available, and they were blocking the main roads in and out of Srebrenica, which all made for problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you've described the hospital. Did the situation in the hospital have an impact on command and control?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, it did, in the sense that the soldiers knew that it was very inadequate and therefore it would be hurting the morale, which would hurt the ability for the commander to lead and control his forces. So in that sense, a hospital being able to take care of a wounded soldier is vital to a defensive operation, or even an offensive operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And generally speaking in Srebrenica, how well were things managed, from what you could observe?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Let me tell you about several incidents. I'll give just a couple of examples and you can ask me if you want me to go further. When we arrived there in Srebrenica, that was the first great example. The refugees were crowding the streets and the civil authorities did not know what to do with them because there were so many, and this problem increased the entire time I was there. The second example is when we were trying to find a secure drop zone, the refugees were mobbing the drop zone sites, interrupting the recovery of the supplies. The third example is we had a special air-drop just to the north of the PTT building and I had organised the local civil police force and some of our own soldiers to quickly secure one pallet that was going to be dropped for our specific uses, particularly radio batteries for the tactical satellite device. The refugees got there before we could because the pallet, unfortunately, landed on the wrong side of the hill and they were all over it. Everything disappeared before the civil police could get there to secure that pallet. The refugees were constantly causing problems with basic military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. I'm going to take those briefly, but one at a time. The air-drops, first of all can you just tell us: Was this Operation Provide Promise?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And your function in relation to that was as a forward air controller?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, why was it necessary, first of all, to drop aid to Srebrenica from the air?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Because ground convoys were not getting in and they were out of supplies, specifically food and medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We saw in the video that air-drops were taking place at night. Why did they take place at night?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Because for two reasons: One, we were concerned about Serb anti-aircraft guns shooting at C-130 aircraft, particularly when they were coming in low for an air-drop; and the second one was that we were worried about Serb artillery actually shelling the drop zone and killing lots of civilians. And I believe there was an incident just before I got in where that actually had happened close to the line of conflict between the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did that ever give rise to problems with fighters actually leaving the lines to get food?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody was out of food, and the fighters had two concerns. One is, of course, trying to hold the line, but also they had their own families that they had to worry about. So their priorities were definitely dual-hatted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the fact that fighters would leave the lines to get food, does that reflect on the command and control situation you described?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if your fighters are not being fed, then they have to fend for themselves. That means that your fighters are deserting to survive and keep their families alive; that means that you don't have a coherent fighting force when you need them, particular in crisis times.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, were you also present when a convoy, a UNHCR convoy, came into Srebrenica and then people were evacuated?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was General Morillon still in Srebrenica then?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: On the ground convoy, yes, he led it in, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have a clip of a video. It's D700. It goes from 00 to 01.31.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: "Tony Birtley, set the stage for us. What is it we're going to see and hear next? "I think we're going to see one of the scenes that will stay with me and I think for the people who saw the video for many, many, many years, and that is the sight of complete and utter desperation of people who simply want to get out of a situation and are prepared to do anything to do that. "I couldn't believe what I was seeing. I think sometimes in journalism there can be wont to steer towards hyperbole, but you could -- there was nothing you could say to describe what was going on, the sheer panic and the desperation of the people. And to see women throw their babies into the back of trucks and hoping that somebody will grab them and take them to safety because the separation, for them, was far better than having the youngster endure starvation and shells bullets. It was terrible to witness. The scenes of people getting angry before the convoy left. The UN heard about it, but they could do nothing. I think people become so desperate, they're prepared to do absolutely anything. I think it's the lowest level of humanity. I think these people are prepared to steal, even kill, to survive, because nobody else is looking after them."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, are those the scenes that you saw in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, particularly the two convoys that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You saw on that video attempts by a man to control the crowd with a gun. Is that something you saw?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, that looked like it was one of the local guards in front of the PTT building, and he is firing his Kalashnikov in the air, trying to control the crowds. Of course they ignored him and pushed right by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So was it possible on that day to control the crowd, from what you could see?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No, the crowd was desperate to get out of there. They were starved, they were sick, and they had no hope, and they were willing to take, you know, tremendous risk, even death or serious injury, in order to get on those trucks. You could see the old women trying to crawl on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, leaving that incident aside, were you also involved in an attempt to evacuate the wounded from Srebrenica by helicopter?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. General Morillon had left the pocket with Major Tucker and his Macedonian warrant officer, and I had come back to find that they were gone and found out I was the senior officer on the ground and was then given the mission to organise this helicopter evacuation of wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We saw earlier today a photograph of you speaking through Senad to a man in a beard. Was that related to that incident?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That sounds like -- that would sound about right, because a key thing that we were trying to do then is get an accurate head count of how many serious injuries -- seriously injured people we actually had to evacuate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So is it right, then, that you were liaising with the War Presidency, or at least a member of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. That -- again, I cannot recall for sure, but looking at the picture and what was going on, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did that evacuation go off safely?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: We had organised the night -- or the day before. We had a very good operations plan. Everybody had specific duties and responsibilities to carry out. With the Bosnian forces, particularly, it was the civil police under Senad -- excuse me, not Senad, but under Zele who were going to use the police to secure the outside of the perimeter. The Canadian military, the one squad within 113 was going to secure the inside of the perimeter. Zele was -- no, excuse me, Senad was going to get the trucks. The UNHCR doctor -- excuse me, the Doctors Without Borders was going to tag the wounded, and I was going to basically be in charge of the operation, making it happen. I also left another officer at the hospital to make sure we got the wounded moving onto the trucks once we got the first evacuation out. We had talked it through, we had rehearsed it, we were ready to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What stopped it going ahead smoothly?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: The morning of the operation I sent the civilian police down to secure the outside of the soccer field perimeter. They moved out smartly and did it. As soon as they arrived, some Serb artillery rounds struck. One police officer was killed and at least two others were wounded. We continued on with the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to refer again to D199. It's page 156, the "War Hospital" book.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Can I have a copy, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. 156. Now, it's the third paragraph, I think. "Major Dudley was with his tactical satellite device beside a concrete wall, partly protected, when one of the shells landed about 60 feet away. The huge craters in the soggy ground suggest to him large-calibre shells shot by a Serb artillery battery. The great accuracy of the strikes makes him think they've been called in by a forward observer with a clear view of the evacuation from the hills above." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is very correct. The shell landed right in the middle of the soccer field, very close to where the air controllers - I believe they were both French - were located right after the first wave of helicopters had taken off.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And your opinion was that the Serbs were actually with a clear of the evacuation of the wounded and the blue helmets were actually shelling the evacuation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Fortunately for us, the first wave of helicopters had already taken off and the trucks that had brought the wounded had also left for the hospital to get the second load. So the only people inside the stadium at that time were the two French air controllers and the Canadian forces. I believe Tony Birtley was also on the ground with his video. The rest of the forces, 113 and a couple of Jeeps, were up against the concrete wall that was very close to the stadium and actually was inside the stadium walls. So we were fortunate we did not have a whole lot of people on the ground when the initial shelling started.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, one thing we're interested here is the damage which can be done by artillery. What sort of a crater was created by the shells?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: This crater was huge, and the key thing I remember, it was almost as big as from where my desk is here to that first table in front of me. And it would be just about as wide, and it was above my head. And that suggested to me either a very large calibre, like a 152-millimetre artillery shell or more likely a huge mortar shell, because they had to have a high angle of trajectory in order to lob it over the hills and into that soccer stadium. And again, they put it right in the middle of that soccer stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can you tell us whether regular high-explosive rounds can actually set fire to objects like buildings?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. High-explosive rounds, particularly with dry wood, can easily start a fire; either grass fire or a forest fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how about tracer fire?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Tracer fire most definitely can start, particularly grass fires, but also forest fires, and it can also start fires inside of buildings if they hit dry wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you see tracer fire being used in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. At that drop zone. You could see it in the video. And I did not get close enough to the front lines at night to see Serb tracer fire, but I would strongly suspect that they had it and used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've referred already to Naser or to Naser Oric. Who, in fact, mentioned him to you, mentioned that name?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: The first time I heard his name was from my keeper/interpreter, Senad. And I asked him who is the commander on the ground that I can coordinate with. And he mentioned Naser as the person to do that with. I then requested --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me take it step by step. Now, do you recall, first of all, the exact words Senad used in these discussions and whether that was in English or in German or what precisely his words were?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I don't remember his words precisely. I requested to meet with the local military commander, and he said that was Oric, Naser. Excuse me, it was just Naser, that's the only term I actually heard the entire time I was there. I requested to meet with him, and he said: I will see if I can arrange a meeting, or words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, do you recall -- apart from Senad - and I'll come to that - do you recall anyone else specifically mentioning Naser? Only if you can remember a specific name.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember anybody else specifically naming Naser as the military commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Or even referring to him, mentioning his name?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: It would be possible, but it wouldn't register as a name that came up in multiple conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now -- and how was he referred to? Was it as Naser or as Naser Oric or Oric?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: The only term I ever remember hearing him referred to as is Naser.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, were you able to verify, apart from anything which Senad said, whether in fact Senad, I don't think you've given his last name, whether Senad ever spoke to Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No, I cannot confirm it. I assumed that he was liaisoning with me because Naser requested him to do so, but I can never verify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Senad, in fact, liaised with other people, didn't he, including members of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Just like that gentleman you saw me talking to with him as the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Senad, you told us, arrived in Srebrenica in -- I think you said January or February 1993. Correct?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you said that you asked him to arrange a meeting with Naser. Was he ever able to arrange that?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I know I requested at least three times that first week I was there to try to meet with the local military commanders, or commander - I don't know which - and he wasn't able to pull it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So in the first week you requested at least three times to meet with either a local military commander or commanders. And Senad said that he would see what he could do, but he didn't actually arrange a meeting with -- between you and Naser. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you ever see Senad in the company of Naser?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No, I did not. Let me state here, I -- while I was in the pocket, I would not have known Naser if I saw him because I didn't have a face with a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would like actually if the witness could now be should D902.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this is dated -- well, it's HQ BH command Kiseljak, 15 March 1993. Period covered last seven days. And that's from the 7th to the 15th March 1993. And it says: "General situation: The area of operations was quiet other than in Sarajevo and the eastern enclaves where the media continues to focus international attention." And if we turn to the second page we see under "Eastern Bosnia" it's written: "The systematic cleansing of the Srebrenica enclave continues in the form of a strong BSA offensive. It appears that the Serbs are advancing from the north and east simultaneously. With the fall of Cerska this week, BSA forces pushed east and south, pressuring Konjevic Polje and Srebrenica respectively. "The situation in Srebrenica is reported as being desperate as civilian refugees are concentrating there. There are a large number of wounded and they are reportedly without medicine and anaesthetics. "(c) the condition of the Srebrenica defense is not clear amid media reports of its imminent collapse." And I'll pause there. This refers to a period when you were in the pocket. Was this the situation, as far as you know, on the 15th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That's a very accurate statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was there, or was there not at the time, some pretty desperate fighting on the front lines?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. And you could see it on the faces of the fighters as they were returning to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you analyse the tactics, if any, that were being used on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And again, I stated, as I stated before, I was very interested to see if they were going to be able to hold the perimeter of Srebrenica, and that was the key reason for analysing and asking exactly how they were defending the pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in fact, is part of what you concluded set out in this manual which you contributed to on the tactics of the different sides in the Bosnian conflict?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: The key term I would like to use is the Muslims were using a term called asymmetric warfare, and they were hitting the Serbs in the one weak spot that they could, which was using surprise, small-unit raiding parties to disrupt their operations. Most of these operations took place at night or very early morning just before dawn to strike when and where they could and as unexpectedly as they could. The only other tactic that the Muslims used were small units going up to the front lines to hold specific parts of the perimeter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you say "asymmetric warfare," what was asymmetric about it?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: The Serbs had overwhelming combined arms power. They had tanks, they had AAA, air defence artillery weapons mounted on vehicles. They had a wide variety of calibres of indirect-fire weapons, both mortars and artillery and multiple rocket launches, and they had supporting aircraft flying over from Serbia dropping bombs on the enclave. All the Muslims had were small arms and some automatic weapons. I saw one tank in town, but it didn't have ammunition. And they had very limited fuel, so it wasn't any good to them even as a transport vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know where they got that tank from?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I'm assuming that they captured it from Serb forces when they surprised them on one of their raids.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, when we speak of tactics on the Muslim side, is this something which were organised tactics or disorganised? How would you characterise it?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I would prefer to use the term "semi-autonomous activities." As I mentioned earlier, their communications were almost non-existent. They had to use couriers, say the commander going around and rounding up his own men or sending men that he had to get other people. And that was the primary ways of communicating on the front lines, too, was sending runners, because they had no land-lines or good FM radios to talk with. And the few devices they did have were not secure, so the Serbs had the capability of intercepting them. So the communications were almost non-existent between different small unit commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in these raids which you've described, are you able to say whether or not they were able to actually hold territory and whether that was one of the aims?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Well, that was one of their biggest weaknesses is that they could not hold turf, particularly along main avenues of approach, because the Serbs could overwhelm them with both indirect and direct fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we just get a time period of which the witness is now referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sellers. Yes, Mr. Jones, could you address this, please, with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps it's a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When -- These observations you made, what time frame would they cover?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: This was the same time frame that I was in Srebrenica, which was 11 March 1993 through 28 March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. And those observations, meaning the raids and holding territory?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, turning to the Serb side now and the Serb military presence around Srebrenica, would you say the Serbs constituted an organised army or not?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. They were an organised fighting force at the brigade level, and I would probably have to say at the division level.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what were their tactics towards Srebrenica when you were there from what you could tell?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Would you like a detailed answer on this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Okay. The Serbs were mostly composed of reserve soldiers with some professional officers leading them. Therefore, they were capable of combined-arms operations if they were kept simple and set peace. And they had developed a very specific way of clearing villages. They would use indirect fire to shell the villages and immediate surrounding area, chasing out all the refugees and destroying what -- a lot of buildings in the process, trying to deny covering concealment to the defending Muslim forces; I will call those light infantry forces. They would then move in and use AAA guns and other direct-fire weapons, say tank rounds, to further pulverise the area, destroying any other covering defences. If they had tear gas available, they would use that also. They would then finally send in their infantry, because they wanted to minimise their casualties, with tanks and other armoured supporting type vehicles to provide direct-fire support to the infantry and finally clear the town and surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in that regard and given your experience there and experience beforehand, would it be perverse to pulverise, as you say, an area which was held by the Muslims but which had been Serb beforehand?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No. If I were a Serb commander on the ground and a town that had been formerly occupied by my people but had been abandoned, captured by the enemy, was now in enemy hands, unless I needed it for my own operations, destroying those buildings would be a legitimate military target because I wanted to deny covering concealment to the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could be shown D976, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And while that's being passed up, did you hear of any accounts of incendiary or inflammable devices being used by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Specifically, the accusation of napalm was used, that they had seen large, burnt-out areas, but I never saw any personal evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you exclude the possibility of its use or you didn't see it?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this document is dated -- is from the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade command, dated 4 February 1993, and it's a short document, so I can read: "With its main forces the special brigade shall extend the attack towards Kunjerac, while with its auxiliary forces it shall coordinate with the 1st Infantry Battalion in carrying out the mission, artillery on request." Now, firstly, how would you understand auxiliary units?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Auxiliary units are not part of the actual unit in question here, the special brigade. They are detachments. And "auxiliary" specifically means to me, as a military term, that these are untrained or paramilitary-type groups that aren't actually part of the organised military force.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how do you understand the expression "artillery on request"?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: When you provide artillery to a unit, you have either indirect support, direct support, reinforcing general support. In this case, artillery on request means that the artillery was in direct support, so all the commander had to do was ask for it and he would receive it. This also tells me that the Serbs had plenty of artillery to spare, since they could afford to give a brigade commander in a specific operation all the artillery you could need.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you establish the location of Serb artillery in the Srebrenica pocket?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I was able to locate at least -- I saw one point -- one directly because it was shooting at me while I was trying to get to an outlying town. I could see where the guns were firing from, I could see the shells impacting close to my location. And then I was able to get reports, multiple reports that confirmed that some from the UNMOs saw Serb artillery on -- it looked like on the Serb side of the Drina to the north of Srebrenica -- excuse me, to the south of Srebrenica, and then in one vicinity Bratunac. So they were using artillery basically all around the pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in observing this, did you get out and about the enclave? And if so, how? How did you move around?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I usually took one of the Belgian or UNMO Jeeps because I didn't want to burn up a lot of fuel and it was also a four-wheel vehicle that would allow me to get off the main hardball road and off onto the little the bunny tracks as I was looking for adequate drop zones. And yes, I did get out and about just about every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And would you say you got out and about more or less or the same as the other UNMOs and UNPROFOR officers there?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: I got out and about probably more than anybody in the enclave, except for Tony Birtley.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about the next exhibit. It's D904, Defence Exhibit 904. And again, HQ BH command, Kiseljak, 29 March 1993. Period covered: Last seven days, 22 to 28 March, 1993. So that would refer to a time period when you were in the enclave, correct?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Let's see. I was there 11 through 28 March, so, yes, it looks like I was there for most of that time, 22 to 28 March, I was there on the ground. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Again, the general situation we can see. I want to actually turn to 3(a), which is on the next page. It says: "Eastern Bosnia. The BSA offensive into the Srebrenica enclave continued its apparently inexorable drive towards the centre, at Srebrenica from the north, south, and south-east. Muslim towns and villages continued to fall in an almost systematic fashion as BiH local commanders attempted to hold the line. The following built-up areas were reported fallen to the Serbs this week: Ljeskovic, Karacici and Gajic. The villages of Osmace and Subin were last reported surrounded by BSA forces. Fighting was reported in and around Zeleni Jadar, with the Serbs in the town itself on 25 March. As of 27 March, however, the town was still in BiH hands." I want to ask you if you're familiar with any of those places; specifically Osmace and Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember those names specifically. I don't remember exactly where they were located on the map, but they were very close and initially they were on the outside perimeter of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was the situation as described there, is that as you recall it? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Very much so. Particularly, that was the last week that I was in Srebrenica, and I remember going out on a road to the south of Srebrenica, trying to recon on what was going on and see if I could get an air-drop out there to feed the refugees who were streaming into Srebrenica, and also hold them out there instead of overcrowding the town. I went out there with a UNHCR representative, and I was told, Don't go, don't go, there's too many Serbs on the road, they're coming this way, you'll get killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before moving on to my next theme, I want to ask you a bit about the public health situation. You've described that in detail, and I think it's accepted mostly that the conditions, at least in the hospital, and elsewhere, were appalling. In fact, did you personally see children arriving at hospital after Serb mortar attacks?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And I recorded one specific incident where I had just delivered or was going to deliver medical supplies from an air-drop to the hospital. And a cart-load of wounded civilians, particularly children, pulled up. And I remember one girl sitting up in the cart, and she was missing her face, basically, from the eyes down. It was all gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were such scenes usual or unusual in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Unfortunately, they were very usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, were medicines dropped as well as food with the air-drops?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes, and I was very concerned about prioritising what medicines came in based on most need.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did those medicines find their way to the hospital, as intended?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Sometimes yes, sometimes no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recall something involving typhoid vaccines?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. That was another painful experience. The same time that we had organised that other special pallet drop to resupply our headquarters with the radio batteries and special food for our own forces, we were also having a typhoid drop because we were very worried about water-borne diseases breaking out and typhoid being one of the key problems. We, along with the batteries I was so desperately wanting to get my hands on, I was also desperately wanting to get this typhoid medicine to administer to the population. Unfortunately, I found out that when the refugees got a hold of the packet, the pallet, that dropped, they also got a hold of the typhoid medicine. And not knowing what it was, they burned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was there a risk, or not, of epidemics at that time?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. And we actually had a form of epidemic in the town. We call it the Srebrenica crud, but it was a bad respiratory flu-like symptom that people would get a really bad cramping in the stomach, they would be throwing up, they would also have diarrhea. And it would really incapacitate them. I ended up with it after I had left the pocket. And several of our members in the group, the international group, also came down with it while they were in Srebrenica. Again, when you have people who are starved and worn out and crowded into dirty, filthy conditions, they are very prone to epidemics breaking out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then do you recall what the death rate was when you were there, the daily death rate?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: It varied upon each day. We would go from five to 20-plus, depending on what had happened that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was it unusual to see people who looked malnourished?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: No, that was the common look. Even our own forces after that second week, since we were on half rations, were looking pretty malnourished at the end of the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if we could go into private session just briefly. I have a question about a specific person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Jones. Let's go to private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've told how you went into Srebrenica with General Morillon's group, and you've referred to General Morillon, his body-guard. Was he often with General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
utterances.text: Yes. He was -- you could say he was glued at the hip with General Morillon. He was his translator and his body-guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recall a Major Pyers Tucker?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY
